title: The Ediacaran Period, Life Before the Cambrian
description: Tonight is about the long stretch of time before the Cambrian, about ninety-six million years of it, and about the first large bodies that left a mark in the rock. It begins at a pale band of limestone in a creek bed in South Australia, and it ends at a single trail in Newfoundland.

It is told through places: a deep, dark sea floor at Mistaken Point, where fronds were kept under volcanic ash; a quarry in Leicestershire, where a schoolgirl and then three schoolboys found a fossil in rock that was thought too old to hold one; a flat, ribbed oval called Dickinsonia; a trail the width of a grain of rice at Nilpena; and a few small white funnels in Namibia, among the first animals to build hard parts.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. Whether the branching fronds were animals is not known. Whether Dickinsonia was an animal rests on a chemical argument that others have questioned. What made some small round holes in the first shells, whether the Namibian reefs grew where they lie, how far the cold spell reached, and why the large bodies thin out near the end are all argued over. Where researchers disagree, it says so.
It stays gentle throughout. Nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and the end of the period is told only as a before and an after, in the rock.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the trail, that's the intended use.

accuracy: Every factual claim traces to a named source, listed below. Where sources disagree, the episode gives the range or both views. Several of the papers could not be read in full, because publisher pages were blocked; for those the narration says aloud that only a summary, a press report or a general reference was read, and the list below marks them.
